note: A second, harder test set for Milestone 5, separate from mock_status_updates.json. Each item is deliberately adversarial -- designed to bait a specific failure mode (over-trusting alarmed tone, under-trusting calm boilerplate, blindly trusting an inflated self-report, etc.) rather than to be a realistic 'typical' update. purpose is author-only documentation, stripped before sending to the model along with the ground_truth_* fields.

updates.purpose: False-positive bait: anxious tone, but the facts describe a fully successful, completed rollout.
updates.update_text: We were a bit worried about this one going in -- lots of moving pieces across 12 services -- but it actually went according to plan: rotation completed 10/29, validated in production 10/30, zero incidents. Just flagging that it felt stressful on our end.
updates.self_reported_rationale: Rated Medium mostly because of how tense the week felt, even though nothing actually went wrong.
updates.ground_truth_note: Completed successfully before the due date with zero incidents. Tests whether the classifier over-indexes on anxious language rather than the actual outcome.

updates.purpose: False-negative bait: calm, content-free reassurance masking a real risk (three weeks of the same non-answer on a due-tomorrow item).
updates.initiative: Data Center Cloud Migration - Final Cutover Readiness
updates.update_text: All good here, nothing new to report.
updates.ground_truth_note: Third consecutive week of identical content-free 'all good' on a complex cutover due tomorrow, with no evidence readiness has actually been confirmed. Tests whether the classifier treats calm boilerplate as automatically safe.
updates.context_note: Prior two weeks' updates on this same ticket were also exactly 'All good here, nothing new to report.' -- not shown to the model, since a single real update wouldn't have that history attached either; this scenario tests judgment from the update's content alone (a due-tomorrow complex cutover with a one-line non-answer).

updates.purpose: Ambiguous blocked-vs-at_risk boundary -- a defensible near-miss either way, used to test whether errors here are treated differently from a miss against on_track.
updates.update_text: Translation vendor says the fix will be done 'soon' -- no confirmed date despite us asking twice this week. Launch is in 4 days.
updates.self_reported_rationale: Vendor is responsive, just vague on timing.
updates.ground_truth_note: No confirmed date plus two unanswered follow-ups plus 4 days of runway reads as stalled, not just at-risk -- but at_risk is a defensible call too, since the vendor is at least responsive. Scored as a near-miss, not a hard failure, if the model says at_risk instead.

updates.purpose: Subtle competing_objectives -- deprioritization stated as a routine decision, not framed as an emergency, with a Low self-report.
updates.update_text: Deprioritized this in favor of the homepage redesign this sprint per the VP's request in last week's standup. Will pick it back up next sprint.
updates.self_reported_rationale: Not urgent work, fine to slip a sprint.
updates.ground_truth_note: A due date one week out with work explicitly paused for another priority, framed calmly by the team but still a real threat to the date. Tests recognition of quiet, routine-sounding deprioritization, not just dramatic 'emergency' language.

updates.purpose: Subtle unowned_escalation -- a risk raised through a slow channel (email) with a moderate self-report, not framed as a crisis.
updates.initiative: Vendor Contract Renewal - Data Processing Addendum
updates.update_text: Flagged a contract risk to the General Counsel's office by email two weeks ago; haven't heard back, sent a follow-up this week.
updates.self_reported_rationale: Waiting on GC, out of our hands.
updates.ground_truth_note: A risk named to leadership two weeks ago with no response, now a second unanswered follow-up -- the escalation channel itself is stalled. Tests whether unowned_escalation is recognized without dramatic framing.

updates.purpose: False-positive bait, mirrored: self-report is High out of policy-driven caution, but the actual content describes a fully completed, signed-off item.
updates.update_text: Rated High per our team policy of auto-flagging anything that touches payments, but there are no open issues: QA passed, staged, and release is scheduled for tomorrow with sign-off from all stakeholders.
updates.self_reported_rationale: Policy requires High rating for any payment-touching change regardless of actual status.
updates.ground_truth_note: Tests whether the classifier blindly inflates severity because the self-report says High, when the update's own content describes a fully signed-off, ready-to-ship item.

updates.purpose: Missing/null self-report plus an empty update on an already-overdue ticket -- data-handling edge case, not just a content-judgment one.
updates.ground_truth_note: No update at all, third week running, on a ticket already a week past its due date. Tests that an empty/null update doesn't break classification and is still read as a strong quiet signal, not treated as 'no data, assume fine.'

updates.purpose: False-positive bait: dramatic incident language, but the incident is fully resolved in the past with no due-date impact.
updates.update_text: Had a scary moment Tuesday -- the rotation script failed on first attempt and threw errors across 40 services. Rolled back immediately, root-caused a config typo, re-ran successfully Wednesday morning, and validated everything. No impact to the 10/29 due date, which we hit.
updates.self_reported_rationale: Rated Medium to reflect that it wasn't smooth, even though we hit the date.
updates.ground_truth_note: The incident is fully resolved, in the past, and the due date was already hit. Tests that dramatic incident language about a resolved past event doesn't trigger a false positive on a currently-fine ticket.
